title: Expansion Cards, Storage, Power Supplies
summary: PCIe, storage speeds, optical capacity, PSU voltages, hot-swap, RAID 5, and video cards.

items: PCIe (PCI Express) is the standard for GPUs and other high-speed cards.
PCIe x16 provides the highest bandwidth for video cards.
PCIe is a serial bus and is faster than older parallel buses.
M.2 is a form factor for NVMe or SATA SSDs.
NVMe is the fastest storage protocol (about 3.5–4 GB/s).
SATA 3 is about 600 MB/s. PATA/IDE is legacy (40-pin, obsolete).
A NIC (Network Interface Card) connects a device to a network.
Fastest to slowest: PCIe (~4.0 GB/s) → M.2/NVMe (~3.5 GB/s) → SATA 3 (600 MB/s) → SATA 2 (300 MB/s) → SATA 1 (150 MB/s) → PATA (legacy).
HDD = mechanical, slower. SSD = no moving parts, faster. NVMe = newest/fastest standard.
Optical drives (DVD, Blu-ray) are declining. Memory cards (SD, microSD, CompactFlash) are for cameras. USB flash drives are portable storage.
Single-sided, single-layer Blu-ray ≈ 25 GB.
Double-sided, single-layer DVD+R ≈ 9–10 GB.
DVD+R/DVD-R single-layer ≈ 4.7 GB.
CD ≈ 700 MB.
A 20 GB video file needs a larger format than single-layer DVD.

blocks.text: Wall outlet is AC. The computer needs DC. The PSU converts AC → DC. Reversing input/output is a common exam mistake.

items: Standard PC voltages: +3.3V DC, +5V DC, +12V DC, −12V DC (rarely used).
Not standard: +4.3V, +8V, +110V as DC rail values.
Wattage varies (100W, 500W, 850W) and must match system needs. Voltage conversion stays AC→DC.
Redundant PSU = backup if the primary fails; critical on servers. Often one on / one standby.
Hot-swappable: power does not need to be turned off before insert/remove (USB, many external drives, some bays).
Hot-swap is not the same as yanking a drive immediately after shutdown while it is still spinning/hot.
Modern internal HDDs do not need a separate external power source; the PSU has capacity.
Match form factor. Secure with at least two screws (one per side; preferably two each side). Do not block airflow with cables.
RAID 5: minimum 3 drives, striping with parity, survives one drive failure.
Rebuild time can be hours to months in enterprise — a real operational challenge.
Discrete video: PCIe x16 is the standard. Can coexist with integrated video (may disable IGP in BIOS).
PCIe cards are usually auto-detected; still install the correct driver.
PCIe x128 is not a real standard. AGP is obsolete. Plain PCI is too slow for video.

title: Operating System Basics
summary: Windows 11 requirements, editions, boot order, file systems, registry, and accounts.

blocks.text: TPM 2.0 is mandatory and is often the upgrade blocker — not just RAM or disk size.

items: Processor: 1.0 GHz or faster, 2 cores minimum.
RAM: 4 GB minimum (8 GB recommended).
Storage: 64 GB minimum (CompTIA spec; Microsoft marketing numbers can be lower).
Display: 720p, 9" minimum. Firmware: UEFI with Secure Boot capable.
Home: local accounts only, no domain join, no BitLocker, no Remote Desktop host.
Pro: domain join, BitLocker, Remote Desktop, Group Policy.
Enterprise: domain-oriented, full feature set.
Windows 11 is 64-bit.
Same OS family and same bitness can upgrade. 32-bit → 64-bit requires a clean install.
Win10 Home → Win11 Pro can be an in-family upgrade path when licensing allows.
1. POST — BIOS/UEFI checks hardware.
2. Boot loader — locates OS files.
3. Kernel load — Windows core loads.
4. Logon — user authentication.
5. Shell/desktop — GUI loads.
Won't start at all → POST/hardware. BSOD during boot → driver/kernel. Stuck at logon → network/auth. Black screen → often display driver.
Internal C: = NTFS. External USB / Mac+Windows = exFAT. Legacy only = FAT32.
A 5 GB file will not fit on FAT32.
Registry is a hierarchical configuration database. Do not edit without a reason; bad edits can prevent boot.
HKLM = hardware, system, services. HKCU = current user settings. System Restore backs up registry.
Administrator = full access. Standard = apps, limited system changes. Guest = very restricted. Service accounts run background services, not interactive logon.
Explicit Deny beats Allow. Group Policy can lock settings company-wide. Use least privilege.

title: Windows Configuration
summary: MMC snap-ins, Event Viewer, registry hives, GPT/MBR, power modes, TRIM vs defrag.

items: eventvwr.msc — Event Viewer
devmgmt.msc — Device Manager (hardware only)
diskmgmt.msc — Disk Management
services.msc — Services
compmgmt.msc — Computer Management
gpedit.msc — Group Policy Editor
msconfig — System Configuration (often launched as msconfig, not a typical .msc exam mix-up).

blocks.text: Device Manager is hardware only: adapters, USB, sound. It is not for apps or services.

items: System log: OS, drivers, reboots. Application: app crashes. Security: logons and permission denials. Setup: install events.
Indexing Options control what Windows Search indexes. File Explorer Options control view settings — different tools.
Task Scheduler runs maintenance, backups, and utilities on a schedule.
Five main hives: HKLM, HKCU, HKCR (file associations), HKEY_USERS (all profiles), HKEY_CURRENT_CONFIG (hardware profile).
MBR: legacy, max 4 primary partitions. GPT: modern, many partitions. UEFI requires GPT.
Boot partition holds boot files. ESP (EFI System Partition) holds BCD on UEFI. WinRE is recovery.
Sleep/standby: RAM stays powered, fast wake. Hibernate: RAM written to disk, slower wake, less power. Shutdown: full power off.
Defragment HDDs. Use TRIM on SSDs (tells the drive which blocks are free). Do not defrag SSDs as a performance habit.

title: Windows Administration
summary: Sysprep, ImageX/DISM, WDS, setup passes, updates, BCD, bootrec, 20 SMB connections.

sections.title: Setup passes (WinPE is not a pass)

blocks.text: WinPE is the environment you boot into. It is not a Windows setup pass.

items: auditSystem — system-wide setup
generalize — strips hardware-specific drivers and SIDs
auditUser — user-specific setup
OOBE — Out-of-Box Experience for the first user

blocks.text:
1. Configure reference PC
2. sysprep /oobe /generalize /shutdown   ← PREPARE first
3. Boot WinPE
4. imagex /capture  or  DISM /Capture-Image   ← CAPTURE
5. Add image to WDS
6. PXE-boot targets
7. WDS deploys image   ← DEPLOY
8. Each PC boots to OOBE
sysprep MUST run before capture. /generalize removes hardware bindings so the image works on other PCs.

items: sysprep = prepare. ImageX/DISM = capture .wim. WDS = deploy over the network.
USMT migrates user data. MAP toolkit assesses hardware. Different jobs.
Insider Program: not on Home. Supported on Pro, Education, Enterprise.
Do not pick “General Availability” as the branch name on this material. Semi-Annual Channel = regular public. LTSC = long-term enterprise. Insider = preview.
Security updates fix vulns (highest priority). Critical = major bugs. Feature updates bump version (21H2 → 22H2). Quality rollups = monthly cumulative. Optional = drivers/extras.
32-bit → 64-bit is clean install only. No in-place, no intermediate stepping stone.
BCD location: legacy MBR → C:\boot. UEFI → ESP.
bootrec /rebuildbcd — rebuild BCD. /fixmbr — MBR. /fixboot — boot sector. /scanos — find Windows installs.
Windows workstation SMB inbound connection limit is 20 — not 25, 30, or 40.

title: Troubleshooting OS and Security
summary: Methodology, Safe Mode, BSOD, CLI tools, malware steps, Task Manager, mobile issues.

items: 1 Identify → 2 theory → 3 test theory → 4 plan/implement → 5 verify and document.
Ask questions before changing things.
Safe Mode (minimal): drivers only. With networking: drivers + network. With Command Prompt: minimal + cmd.
Win10/11: Shift+Restart → Troubleshoot → Advanced → Startup Settings → F4/F5/F6.
Order: Startup Repair → System Restore → bootrec → SFC → Reset this PC → reimage.
Note the stop code. Safe Mode → roll back driver → uninstall recent software → restore → memory diagnostic.
DRIVER_IRQL_NOT_LESS_OR_EQUAL → bad driver. PAGE_FAULT → RAM. SYSTEM_SERVICE_EXCEPTION → service crash.

sections.title: Malware, AV, SFC vs regedit, activation

blocks.text: Malware order: identify/verify first, then quarantine, remediate, educate. Do not skip identify.

items: Antivirus definitions: daily, not weekly. New malware is constant.
SFC repairs system files. regedit edits the registry. Do not use regedit to “fix” SFC-class corruption.
Unactivated Windows: personalization (wallpaper) limited. Apps, updates, and browsing still work.
Tabs: Processes, Performance, App History, Startup, Services, Details.
High CPU/RAM: identify in Processes, end or uninstall. 100% disk: check indexing, search, failing HDD, or missing TRIM on SSD. Network spike: identify the process.
Battery drain: limit background apps. Overheating can throttle or shut down. WWAN is cellular; Wi-Fi is local wireless. Auto-connect to open Wi-Fi is a risk.

title: DNS and DHCP
summary: DORA, APIPA, ports, DNS records, forwarders, and failure symptoms.

items: Ports: UDP 67 (server) and UDP 68 (client).
DORA: Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge.
APIPA 169.254.x.x means DHCP failed. It is not a usable routed address.
Leases expire; clients renew. Rogue DHCP is a security issue; DHCP snooping / authorized servers help.
3-2-1 backup is a backup rule, not a DHCP setting.
DNS maps names to IPs.
A = IPv4. AAAA = IPv6 (four As, larger address).
CNAME = alias. MX = mail. PTR = reverse. TXT = text/SPF-style records.
A forwarder sends unresolved queries to another DNS server.
Name fails but IP works → DNS. Both fail → network path.

title: RAID, NAS, SAN, backups
summary: RAID 0/1/5/10, NAS vs SAN, and the 3-2-1 backup rule.

rows: N/A — any disk loss kills the array
Often cannot use volume until rebuild finishes
Can often stay online during rebuild

blocks.text: RAID 5: blocked during rebuild on this study guide. RAID 10: accessible during rebuild because of mirrored pairs.

items: Hardware RAID uses a controller card; software/virtual RAID is OS-based. Servers often have onboard RAID; desktops may need a card.
RAID presents disks as one logical drive. RAID is not a backup.
NAS: Ethernet (often 1–2.5 Gb), sometimes USB. File sharing and media for home/SMB. Ethernet can bottleneck. WD common; Synology can lock to vendor drives.
SAN: high-speed enterprise (Fibre Channel, LUNs). CapEx hardware vs cloud OpEx.
3-2-1: 3 copies, 2 media types, 1 offsite. RAID = local redundancy. Backups = disaster recovery. You want both.

title: Critical weak areas
summary: Ten high-miss items from class drills: sysprep, DNS records, RAID rebuild, TPM, AC/DC, and more.

items: 1. sysprep first, then ImageX/DISM capture, then WDS deploy. /generalize is the key switch.
2. A = IPv4. AAAA = IPv6.
3. IP works, name fails = DNS. Neither works = network.
4. tracert = path. pathping = path + loss.
5. RAID 5 cannot be used during rebuild (this guide). RAID 10 can.
6. TPM 2.0 is mandatory for Windows 11.
7. Wall = AC, PC = DC, PSU converts AC→DC.
8. Workstation SMB cap = 20 connections.
9. 169.254.x.x = APIPA = DHCP failed.
10. Antivirus definitions update daily, not weekly.

title: Cabling and Connectors
summary: Twisted pair categories and speeds, 100 m limit, T568A/B, fiber vs copper, coax, PoE, and cabling tools.

items: UTP (unshielded) is the default LAN cable; STP adds shielding against EMI.
RJ-45 is the 8P8C connector for Ethernet twisted pair.
Cat 5e: 1 Gb/s at 100 m. Cat 6: 10 Gb/s but only to 55 m (100 m at 1 Gb/s). Cat 6a: 10 Gb/s at 100 m. Cat 7: 10 Gb/s, shielded, 100 m.
All Ethernet twisted pair: maximum run 100 m before signal attenuation.
T568A and T568B are the two wiring orders for the 8 wires; use one standard on both ends (straight-through).
Crossover cable (T568A on one end, B on the other) is legacy — modern NICs auto-detect with Auto-MDIX.
Fiber uses light: immune to EMI, no crosstalk, longest distances, highest cost.
Single-mode fiber (SMF): laser, long distance (campus/ISP backbone), small core (about 9 micron).
Multimode fiber (MMF): LED/VCSEL, shorter runs inside buildings, larger core (50/125 or 62.5/125 micron), orange/aqua jacket.
Fiber connectors: LC (small, latching — most common today), SC (push-pull square), ST (bayonet twist, legacy).
Coaxial (RG-6 for TV/satellite/internet drops, RG-59 legacy video): F-connector screws on; BNC twists/locks (older networks, CCTV).
PoE delivers DC power over the same Ethernet cable that carries data.
802.3af (PoE): up to 15.4 W at the switch.
802.3at (PoE+): up to 30 W.
802.3bt (PoE++/4PPoE): up to about 60 W (Type 3) / 100 W (Type 4).
Powers APs, IP cameras, VoIP phones — no outlet needed at the device.
Crimper attaches RJ-45 ends; punch-down tool terminates cable into patch panels/keystone jacks (110 block).
Cable tester verifies pinout; wire map tester catches split/incorrect pairs. Tone generator + probe traces a cable in a bundle.
Loopback plug tricks a NIC into thinking it is connected — quick port test.
Common faults: wrong pinout (T568 mismatch), bent/broken cable, runs over 100 m, EMI near motors/fluorescent lights (use STP or fiber), crosstalk from untwisted pairs left too long at the connector.
